item.title: The Question About Transgender Youth That Adults Struggle to Answer
item.description:
Transgender

The Question About Transgender Youth That Adults Struggle to Answer

When a bullied trans teen asks whom she's harming, the answer is clear—even if adults can't always see it.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • Adolescents bullied over gender nonconformity are told to change; many ask only to be left alone.
  • Being disbelieved about your own inner experience is a distinct, documented form of harm.
  • Research links stigma and rejection to elevated distress among gender-diverse young people.
  • Having at least one accepting adult is associated with markedly lower risk among LGBTQ youth.

Over the years, I have sat with many bullied adolescents. What follows is a composite drawn from those hours; no single patient is depicted, and identifying details do not belong to any individual. But the question at the center of this article was asked, essentially in these words, and I have never stopped thinking about it.

Picture a 15-year-old whose tears fall faster than she can speak. She has endured years of teasing, degradation, and profound loneliness—not because she has done anything to anyone, but because she will not perform a role that does not fit her. She was assigned male at birth; she knows herself to be a girl. The world around her keeps issuing the same instruction: Change. Become a real man.

She has never asked anyone else to change. Her request, when you listen closely, is startlingly small: "I am not asking them to talk to me. I am asking them not to talk to me. Not to insult me on my way to class." She is asking for negative space—to be left alone.

And then, voice breaking, the question: "There are so many 'real men' out there. Why can she not choose not to be one? Whom is she harming?"

Notice the pronoun. This is how she experiences herself. And notice the question, because I have yet to hear an adult answer it well.

The Harm of Being Disbelieved

Philosophy has a name for one part of what this adolescent experiences. Miranda Fricker (2007) calls it testimonial injustice: being wronged specifically in one's capacity as a knower—having your account of your own experience discounted before it is even considered.

Whatever position an adult holds on wider questions, something distinct happens to a young person who is told, daily, that the person she experiences herself as is not real. She is not merely being teased about something. She is being told that her account of her own inner experience does not deserve to be heard as evidence at all.

The predicament is a genuine double bind. If she performs the role demanded of her, she purchases social safety at the cost of her inner life. If she declines, she pays in daily degradation and isolation. Neither door leads anywhere good, and she did not build the corridor.

What the Research Shows About Social Belonging

The need to belong is not a preference; it is one of the most fundamental human motivations, and its frustration carries serious psychological costs (Baumeister & Leary, 1995). Neuroimaging research has found that social exclusion engages some of the same brain regions involved in the distress of physical pain, although shared activation does not imply identical experiences (Eisenberger, Lieberman, & Williams, 2003). The finding nevertheless fits what excluded people report: Rejection hurts.

For young people like the one in this composite, the research points to a crucial distinction. Meyer’s (2003) minority-stress framework originally described how prejudice, rejection, concealment, and other stigma-related stressors contribute to mental-health disparities among sexual minorities; subsequent research has extended the framework to transgender and gender-diverse people (Hendricks & Testa, 2012). And the protective findings mirror the harmful ones: Family acceptance in adolescence is associated with better mental health in young adulthood (Ryan et al., 2010), and transgender youth who could use their chosen name in more contexts reported fewer depressive symptoms and less suicidal ideation (Russell et al., 2018).

These are associations, not guarantees. But they all point the same direction: The environment is not merely the backdrop to their suffering. It can be one of its important sources.

On Her Withdrawal

Her loneliness deserves careful reading. Withdrawing from people who hurt you is understandable self-protection, and adults should resist pathologizing a child for avoiding her tormentors. At the same time, isolation in a bullied adolescent is never something to romanticize; disconnection is among the conditions under which despair grows, and a young person's retreat is a signal that the adults around her have work to do.

The goal is not to demand she be more resilient—resilience-talk too often serves to relocate the problem to the victim—but to make connection safe enough that she no longer needs the fortress. Even one accepting adult is not a small thing: in a large national survey, LGBTQ youth who reported having at least one accepting adult were 40 percent less likely to report a suicide attempt in the past year (The Trevor Project, 2019).

The Question, Answered

Adults disagree, sometimes fiercely, about clinical and policy questions involving transgender youth, and those debates will continue. But her question is not about any of that, and it does not need to wait for those debates to resolve. She is not asking anyone to change their beliefs. She is asking to walk to class without being degraded.

So let me answer her question as plainly as I can, because she deserves a plain answer. In the situation she is describing—existing as herself and asking not to be insulted—whom is she harming? No one. And whatever an adult believes about anything else, no belief licenses the daily tormenting of a child. On that, there is nothing left to debate.

Her question deserves to be turned around, gently, toward the rest of us: What is the harm in leaving her in peace? What, exactly, would it cost us to let her be?

I have never heard a good answer to that one, either.

If you are a young person in distress, or an adult worried about one: in the U.S., call or text 988, or reach the Trevor Project (for LGBTQ youth) at 1-866-488-7386 or thetrevorproject.org; outside the U.S., findahelpline.com lists local services.

item.title: Making First Impressions on People We’ve Known for Years
item.description:
Authenticity

Making First Impressions on People We’ve Known for Years

Why the people who love us don’t need our best version

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • We often perform for close friends, aiming to present our "best selves" even when it's unnecessary.
  • The Trinidadian concept of "lime" values unplanned, authentic gatherings over polished presentations.
  • True intimacy grows when we stop rehearsing and simply share our ordinary, unfiltered selves.

I’m very good at making first impressions on people I’ve known for years. Even with my closest friends, I feel the need to present my best self at all times. And that takes preparation.

Text before you call. Let’s find a time. Thursday works. Two o’clock is perfect. Give me 20 minutes, and I’ll become the version of myself I’d like you to meet. I’ll put on a better shirt. I’ll remember my funniest stories. I’ll shake off whatever disappointment or irritation I’ve been carrying around all day. By the time you arrive, you’ll be seeing someone carefully assembled.

Recently I realized that I’ve spent years becoming presentable. The problem is that I may also have become a little unfindable.

Kacheve Stafford
Source: Kacheve Stafford, used with permission

The Self We Edit

While recording an episode of 50 Words for Snow, the podcast where my co-host Emily John Garces and I explore words that have no direct English equivalent, we spoke with Kacheve Stafford, co-host of The Healing Room podcast, who grew up in Trinidad and Tobago. He introduced us to the Trinidadian word lime.

To lime isn’t simply to socialize. It’s to gather. You hear music coming from someone’s house and wander over. A pot is already cooking. Friends arrive without warning. Somebody brings drinks. Somebody else starts dancing. The gathering grows naturally because the point isn’t to host an event. The point is simply to be together. Kacheve described it as a way of building family and community, where people don’t need an invitation to belong.

What fascinated me wasn’t just the word itself. It was the assumption underneath it. Nobody has 20 minutes to become impressive. Nobody gets time to rehearse. You answer the door as the person you happen to be that day.

My own social life often feels like the opposite. I schedule weeks in advance. I think about what to wear, what to bring, whether we’ll be interesting enough, funny enough, rested enough. Even dinner with close friends can start to feel like a small performance.

Becoming Findable

I’m starting to realize the people closest to us probably don’t need our best stories. They don’t need us at our funniest, our most productive, or our most charming. They may simply want access to the person who’s having an ordinary Tuesday. The one who’s tired. The one whose kitchen isn’t clean. The one who answers the door before she’s had a chance to become someone else.

Listening to Kacheve describe liming made me realize that community may not be built by showing each other our highlights. It may be built by interrupting one another’s ordinary lives. There is something deeply trusting about assuming you can arrive exactly as you are and that whoever opens the door will be glad you came anyway.

I’m not sure I’m ready for surprise visitors. The thought still makes me a little anxious. But I do wonder what it would be like to become the sort of person who hears music and walks toward it instead of checking the calendar first. Or the sort of person who leaves the door unlocked while the pot is on.

Perhaps intimacy begins the moment we stop rehearsing for the people who already love us.

item.title: What We’ve Been Getting Wrong About Depression
item.description:
Depression

What We’ve Been Getting Wrong About Depression

What if depression is not a brain imbalance but a whole-body response to threat

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • Depression is likely not caused by serotonin imbalance.
  • It is often a natural autonomic nervous system response to threat, stuck due to lack of a safe environment.
  • Many aspects of body, mind, relationships, and environment may need to be worked with in therapy.
  • Work is needed beyond the scope of therapy to create a more supportive and safer environment for us all.
Source: Bianca van Dijk / Pixabay

What do we know about depression? We can list its symptoms, such as low mood, low energy, slowing of thought and movement, loss of concentration, and loss of pleasure and interest in activities. There is also a disruption of our patterns of appetite and sleep, and negative, hopeless, and, at worst, suicidal thoughts. We lose the ability and desire to socialize with others.

But what exactly is depression? Based on 30 years of clinical work, I am convinced that depression is a normal and understandable biological response to threat which has become “stuck.”

Our human nervous system responds to danger and life-threat not just with fight, flight, or freeze responses (fear-arousal), but also with fear-collapse—a sudden shutdown of energy production throughout the body. These two aspects of our fear system can be best understood by looking at the context in which they evolved. When a predator attacks its prey, the prey goes into fear-arousal—running or fighting to help it escape. However, if this response fails, an older threat response shuts down the body and the prey collapses, as we can see when a cat catches a mouse.

This fear-collapse—the same biological mechanism as a faint[1], but without full loss of consciousness—stops the predator’s attack. This can lead to a window of opportunity for escape, triggering a sudden switch back into fight or flight (you may have seen a mouse escaping after a cat has got bored with its inactivity).

We share this fear response with mice and the rest of the animal world[2], but it evolved in response to relatively brief attacks and chases[3], and where life-threatening danger is continuous, and no place of safety can be reached, our fear system cannot deactivate or reset. This can leave us habitually responding with fear-arousal or fear-collapse to any level of threat—real or imagined.

Humans are intensely social animals, for whom expulsion from the group was a life-threatening danger, so our fear-system is also wired-up to react to social threats (e.g., rejection, abandonment, bullying, loss of status) as if these were physical attacks, potentially triggering fear-collapse. Observing my own fear responses has led me to reflect that we experience this drop in energy not only as a total physical collapse, but also (for less than life-threatening dangers) as a partial shutdown, just as we can experience a full faint, and also various levels of “feeling faint.”

Threat-induced shutdown (fear-collapse) would appear to be the biological mechanism underlying depression. This theory adequately explains our experience of depression. The shutdown is brought about by a drop in heart rate and blood pressure, which starves our cells of glucose and oxygen. This disables the cell respiration process whereby mitochondria convert glucose and oxygen into the energy that powers each cell.

This means that muscle cells stop working; we are physically debilitated. Brain cells controlling social engagement and thinking are also disabled—hence the loss of the desire and ability to relate to others and the loss of concentration and slowing of thought that is seen in depression. The body’s lack of energy ensures that whatever thinking capacity remains is negative and hopeless. The shutdown also affects the cells of the digestive tract, severely affecting appetite, and all of these impacts lead inevitably to the loss of our sense of pleasure in life.

Lack of understanding can stigmatize depression sufferers. In the past, this very real energy loss was often treated as imaginary (“it’s all in your head”). More recently, the commonly accepted explanation that it is caused by a serotonin imbalance in the brain has been found to be unsubstantiated, though antidepressants can provide temporary relief, which can open up the possibility of working with a therapist for those with more severe depression. The fear-collapse theory points to an alternative biological basis for the symptoms of depression which aligns with lived experience, social and environmental causation, and trauma-informed clinical practice.

In the contest between prey and predator, the way out of fear-collapse is back through fear-arousal. If the predator’s attention is distracted, creating a window of opportunity, there can be a sudden metabolic shift from collapse into hyper-arousal, which can provide the energy for an escape to a place of safety where the fear system can reset.

This shift out of fear-collapse can be activated when therapists help their clients get in touch with anger that has previously been inaccessible or help them reconnect with sensations in their limbs linked to past reactions to danger. These approaches reactivate fear-arousal responses, which can reverse the depressive paralysis of chronic fear-collapse and restore normal vitality.

However, the key factor in switching off our fear responses is safety. The fear system can only deactivate if we can find safe places in which our body can relax. In a world of social disconnection, job insecurity, over-monitored employees, over-tested schoolchildren, collapsing care services, social media lynch-mobs, fear-driven politics and government-created “hostile environments,” safe places where we can truly relax are disappearing.

Depression is not some sort of defect in the individual sufferer—a sense of safety depends on the environments in which we live and work. Along with anxiety, depression arises from normal biological responses to threat, which become stuck and cannot deactivate because the context of our lives is sensed to be insufficiently safe. By giving full attention to a client’s external circumstances, as well as their hard-wired reactions to threat, therapists play an important role in the alleviation of depression, but ultimately, the solution to the scourge of depression which affects so many of us lies in the responsibility we hold individually and collectively to create a society in which every person can feel safe and secure.

item.title: Are Women Satisfied Supporting a Stay-at-Home Boyfriend?
item.description:
Gender

Are Women Satisfied Supporting a Stay-at-Home Boyfriend?

How salary and societal trends have altered relational stereotypes.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • Traditional marital models involve men working to support his family.
  • Contemporary financial realities include more women than men in the workforce.
  • A stay-at-home boyfriend is viewed differently than a working husband on paternity leave.
  • Working women cohabiting with unemployed boyfriends often leave for a working partner.

Many of us grew up in an era of commercials, ads, and stereotypes of men being the breadwinners and “bringing home the bacon.” Today, many women bring home the bacon, too. The surge of women in the workforce compared with men is a documented reality.[i] Some women have become the breadwinner within their own families, which is viewed as more acceptable than in generations past. This may be due to more opportunities in female-dominated professions, artificial intelligence replacing jobs, or decreased social stigma toward unemployed or between-jobs men.

Yet in contemporary times, a working woman’s role often extends beyond supporting a “house husband” who stays home temporarily to help raise children—often facilitated by formal paid paternity leave from a job. Many women support stay-at-home boyfriends—but perhaps not the long term.

Source: Image by Alexander from Pixabay

The Boyfriend Bed and Breakfast Model

Many contemporary young people in romantic relationships choose not to cohabit until marriage, guided by the sentiments of family, friends, and their faith. But for women who choose to support an unemployed live-in boyfriend, this arrangement affects both partners. Because in contrast to temporarily supporting a working husband who takes a break to care for young children, the “house boyfriend” model involves a woman providing board and lodging free of charge. Yet how does this arrangement affect future family planning? Is it sustainable personally and socially? And how do able-bodied men feel about this new role of dependence?

Modern Men and Family Values

Many men embrace traditional ideas about marital and paternal responsibilities, including the role of supporter and provider. They want to be successful both personally and professionally, gainfully employed and socially satisfied. Masculine pride survives and thrives in many cases, as men endeavor to be workplace assets and a hero at home. Yet in modern expectations and trends, there are differences both culturally and socially. The stay-at-home boyfriend relationship is more common among younger couples, who are cohabitating but not married. Accordingly, when the uneven financial burden creates relational discomfort, women face the choice of whether to stay in the relationship or leave to pursue a more financially stable man.

Female Breadwinning and Relational Health

Research has examined the relational health of married couples where the wife makes more than the husband,[ii] as well as how cultural and societal circumstances affect the way a man feels about having a wife who out-earns him.[iii] Other research includes the specific example of unmarried cohabiting daters where the woman brings home the paycheck. Lacking situational permanence in the form of marriage or family responsibilities, and assuming the absence of abusive or coercive factors, working women have a choice. Instead of continuing to share hard-earned income with a stay-at-home boyfriend, they can opt to replace the unemployed partner with a working man. And according to research, many women do.

Gigi Foster and Leslie S. Stratton (2021) investigated the effects of female breadwinning on relational health and stability.[iv] They acknowledge the importance of social norms, reporting that men have been the primary breadwinners in most homes since the end of World War II, and that violations of this norm can be stressful on partnerships. In examining whether this is still the case, they reviewed more recent data from Australia and the United States, finding a more modest link between female breadwinning and relationship health and stability for mixed-gender couples than in the past. Foster and Stratton also note that problems caused by female breadwinning relationships exist mainly within couples who are cohabiting, particularly for younger people, as well as less educated men. They conclude that although their results suggest that social norms may be weakening, relationship satisfaction is still affected by “mating market dynamics.”

Regarding the applicability of their results, Foster and Stratton report evidence that in Australia, cohabiting women who out-earn their partners end up re-partnering with men who earn more than they do; this may not be true in the United States, due to different economic conditions. Yet research like this highlights the fact that working women have that opportunity, which, especially in an economy where it is increasingly challenging to make ends meet, is viewed as an attractive and often necessary option.

item.title: Trust: The Foundation of AI Adoption
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Trust: The Foundation of AI Adoption

How company culture and communication drive employee acceptance of new tech.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • Communication is one of the most important and most overlooked areas of corporate culture.
  • When organizations take action, they need to be consistent, so every employee is being treated fairly.
  • Employees want leaders who make them feel safe within the organization and within their teams.
Source: Joshua Hoehne / Unsplash

There's a wealth of information circling about what makes a good AI tool, how to install them, and how to use them effectively within an organization. Everyone is focused on the tools themselves: which are the right ones to choose, how to use them, and how to set them up. But as with most new technologies, we often overlook the most important factor: the people who will be using them. Very few companies are focused on the people and how they feel about the tools they’re going to interact with and adopt.

Transformation and adoption best practices continue to show that it doesn’t matter how much money you spend on a tool or a technology system; if the end users don’t adopt it, use it, and embrace it, it’s ultimately worth nothing. Adoption of technology systems is traditionally focused on helping employees to understand what they are doing in the new system, why they are doing it, how it will change their job, and what the benefit of that change brings to them and the organization as a whole. This allows employees to engage with a new tool, know where to get more information, and feel confident using it.

There is something unique, though, when it comes to an AI project: trust. With AI, we are often asking colleagues to use a tool to improve their jobs, teach that tool how to do their jobs, or use a tool to potentially look for ways to replace their jobs, so they can focus on other high-value-add activities. Employees need to have trust in their organization, trust in their leaders, and trust in the overall process for this to work. When a company says they will not use AI to replace employees, employees need to know they are being honest.

Unfortunately, trust is not something that we can build in one day. It’s something that takes months and even years of direct action. Research by Gallup, a global analytics and advisory company focused on workplace research, found that “only 23 percent of U.S. employees strongly agree that they trust the leadership of their organization.”1 That creates a big hill for many companies to climb as they begin to build trust with their employees.

Trust echoes in the things that we say, the actions we take, and all aspects of the culture of an organization. Many companies may have an uphill battle to build trust in their employee base, which will be key to successful AI implementations.

There are three key ways that organizations can build trust with their employees:

1. Communication

Communication is one of the most important and most overlooked areas of corporate culture. For employees to trust their organization, the communications they receive must be clear and authentic. Employees know when leaders are not being honest or not sharing the full set of information.

Communication also needs to be a two-way street, sharing with employees, but also listening to them so that they feel seen and heard. Gallup research shows that “employees who say their manager is always willing to listen to work-related problems are 4.2 times as likely to strongly agree that they trust the leadership of their organization.”1

2. Consistency

When organizations take actions, they need to be consistent, so that every employee feels that they are being treated fairly. It is important that everyone feels that they have a fair shot at promotions, development opportunities, and, when needed, that discipline is consistently applied. The organization also needs to do what they say they will and be consistent in their actions so employees can trust that what is shared at a strategic level will play out in day-to-day activities.

The Stanford Social Innovation Review notes in an article on how organizations build trust that, “If your action or decision turns out to be a mistake, own it. People see what’s happening, even if they don’t say it. It may be hard in those moments to not get defensive or shift the focus from impact to intentions. But it is in these moments when there is real opportunity to build trust.”2

3. Safety

Employees want leaders who make them feel safe within the organization and within their teams. They want to be safe to share their opinions without fear of repercussions. This echoes the earlier point around communication and whether they can share in a two-way format. Safety also applies to workplace deliverables and processes. Are employees safe to explore new paths forward that may lead to potential rework or failure? Finally, are they safe with their managers and peers to know that those colleagues have their back and offer the best intentions for them as they work through development or other challenges that teams face?

Only when an organization has created a culture of trust, good communication, consistent actions, and employee safety will it be able to successfully implement projects based on mutual trust, like an AI implementation. For that employee to teach a machine to do their job, trust is the key factor in the relationship. This will alleviate their fears as they know the company has created an environment that supports them.

An article by Harvard Business Review on the neuroscience of trust tells us that “the effect of trust on self-reported work performance was powerful. Respondents whose companies were in the top quartile indicated they had 106 percent more energy and were 76 percent more engaged at work than respondents whose firms were in the bottom quartile. They also reported being 50 percent more productive, which is consistent with our objective measures of productivity from studies we have done with employees at work.”3

Trust is the secret sauce for corporate culture, especially when it comes to AI, but it is more than words on the wall. Trust is built with everyday actions between employees and their leadership.
